chapter_theme: The minister is defined by what he can do: judge means and time, split and join alliances, unite innate acuity with learning and with the ways of the world. The chapter also assigns him a duty to speak even to a king who won't listen, and warns that a false minister is worse than a multitude of enemies.
structure_note: Parimelazhagar divides the chapter: the minister's qualities (631-635), his distinction (636), his conduct (637-638), and the faults of ministers to be discarded (639-640). He ties the five limbs in 631 to Sanskrit treatises' limbs of counsel.

631.reading: A minister is one excellent in means, timing, method and the difficult task itself.
631.nuance: Manakkudavar makes this concrete in a military way: the hard task is seizing another's realm, the means elephants and horses, and the time a season with water and shade. The verse itself says nothing so specific.

632.reading: A minister is one excellent in five things together, including resolve, protecting the people, learned knowing and labour.
632.nuance: வன்கண் is hard-heartedness when it condemns impostors in 276, but here it is a qualification for office. The word's moral value depends on where it is pointed.

positions.position: This verse lists four, and 'the five' are those of 631. He criticises those who split items here to reach five.
positions.quote: மேற்சொல்லிய அங்கங்கள் ஐந்துடனே திருந்த உடையானே அமைச்சனாவான்

positions.position: The five are named in this verse, including the guarding of the senses, and are needed before one becomes a minister.
positions.quote: அஞ்சாமையும், குடிகாத்தலும், இந்திரியங்களைக் காத்தலும், நூல் முகத்தானறிதலும், முயற்சியும்

633.reading: A minister is one able to divide others, keep his own side close, and bring back those who have broken away.
633.nuance: The verse states three skills of division and joining, with no moral comment. Kalaignar's '(for the nation's good)' and his 'those who reformed' are moral framing added by him. Parimelazhagar links two of them to Sanskrit terms.

634.reading: A minister is one able to discern, to act after weighing, and to speak in a way that settles the matter.
634.nuance: ஒருதலையாச் சொல்லல் doesn't name its audience. For Parimelazhagar the settling speech is aimed at the parties being divided or joined, and for Manakkudavar it settles doubtful matters, so eloquence here is persuasion on one view and judgement on the other.

635.reading: One who knows what is right, whose speech is rich and settled, and who always knows the ways of doing things is the companion for deliberation.
635.nuance: Virtue comes first in the list, in a chapter otherwise about competence. But Parimelazhagar narrows it to 'virtues done by the king', which makes it knowledge of duties more than the minister's own goodness.

636.reading: What over-subtle scheme can stand before those who have keen native intelligence together with treatises?
636.nuance: Parimelazhagar names மதிநுட்பம் first since it must be given by the divine, leaving effort to the learning alone. His contrast of natural and artificial knowledge is a useful frame for the next verse. He also defends the text அதிநுட்பம் against அதினுட்பம், 'finer than that', the sense Manakkudavar's gloss gives; the verse's point survives either way.

637.reading: Even after knowing the method of doing a thing, act with knowledge of how the world goes.
637.nuance: செயற்கை and இயற்கை are opposed: the made and the given. In this verse a treatise's knowledge is the artifice and the world is the nature, which is a surprising way to rank them.

positions.position: Treatise methods must fit the prevailing ways of the world, or the world will blame them.
positions.quote: நூல் நெறியே ஆயினும் உலக நெறியோடு பொருந்தாதன செய்யற்க

positions.position: 'The world' means the court: the character of kings and the standing of their retinue.
positions.quote: உலகநடை அறிதலாவது அரசர் சீலமும் பரிவாரத்திலுள்ளார் நிலைமையும் அறிதல்.

638.reading: Though the king destroys wise counsel and himself knows nothing, the one at his side is bound to tell him what is good for him.
638.nuance: The word for the minister here is உழையிருந்தான், 'the one close by'. Duty arises from nearness, and Parimelazhagar adds that the world will lay the king's fall at the silent minister's door.

positions.position: அறிகொன்று means destroying the understanding of those who advise, even with contempt.
positions.quote: அறிந்து சொல்லியாரது அறிவையும் அழித்து அரசன் தானும் அறியானே ஆயினும்

positions.position: He splits the phrase differently: 'let the king know' what the minister said, and even if he knows nothing, the minister must speak.

639.reading: Better seventy crore enemies than a minister at one's side who plots harm.
639.nuance: Parimelazhagar's reason is that open enemies can be guarded against, but the one inside cannot. 'Seventy crore' is his example of a huge number, not a figure with meaning.

640.reading: Though they plan things properly, those without practical capacity do only what comes to no conclusion.
640.nuance: A good plan is not enough. Parimelazhagar splits capacity into knowing remedies for obstacles and being firm in oneself, so this anticipates the chapter on firmness in action.

links.note: 373 sets one's own understanding above study, and 636 asks for both at once: native acuity with treatises. Taken together, the opposition in 373 is not the Kural's last word on learning and nature.
140 calls the learned ignorant if they can't move in step with the world; 637 turns this into an instruction for statecraft. The Virtue book's moral rule becomes a professional one.
889 says an inner enemy holds ruin even when small as a sesame fragment; 639 gives the same inner enemy a face at the king's side and a scale, seventy crore outer foes.

source_issues: 639: The verse reads பக்கததுள் (likely பக்கத்துள்), and Parimelazhagar's lemma has ஓரேழுபதுகோடி. He also notes variant readings. Manakkudavar's commentary is marked as not aligned.
